title: Running stitch
subtitle: An even dashed line and the base for many other stitches
excerpt: Running stitch passes the needle in and out of the fabric along a line, leaving an even row of dashes. It is the first stitch most people learn and the foundation that whipped, laced, and double running stitches are built on.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), plain sewing and outline stitches (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), running stitch entry.

glossaryTerms.definition: The drawn or traced line on the fabric that guides where the stitches go.

content.text: Running stitch passes the needle in and out of the fabric along a

, leaving a row of even dashes with even gaps between them. It makes a light dotted outline on its own, and it is the base row for whipped, laced, and double running stitches. Because the thread only sits on the surface for short lengths, it uses very little thread on the back.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 2 strands for a fine line, 3 for a bolder one

content.text: Draw a straight line on the fabric. Bring the needle up at the start of the line (point A).
Insert the needle a short, even distance ahead (point B) and bring it up the same distance ahead again (point C), leaving a gap the same length as the stitch.
On firm fabric you can load several stitches onto the needle at once, weaving the tip in and out before pulling through. Keep each stitch and each gap the same length.
Pull through gently so the line lies flat. Carry on to the end of the line, checking that the dashes stay even.

items.symptom: The dashes and gaps look uneven
items.cause: Stitch and gap lengths are being judged by eye and drifting.
items.fix: Pick one length for both the stitch and the gap and hold to it. On evenweave you can count the fabric threads to keep them exact.

items.symptom: The fabric puckers along the line
items.cause: The thread is being pulled too tight as each stitch is drawn through.
items.fix: Keep the hoop drum-tight and pull each stitch only until it lies flat. The thread should rest on the fabric, not draw it up.
